nameStory: The Persian walnut gets its name from ancient trade routes that brought these valuable nuts from Persia (modern-day Iran) westward to Europe and beyond. Though also called 'English walnut' because English merchants popularized the trade, 'Persian walnut' better reflects its true Middle Eastern origins in the mountains of Central Asia.
description: Persian walnut is a medium to large deciduous tree that can reach 50-80 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It's the species that produces the familiar grocery store walnuts we eat, with smooth gray bark and large compound leaves. While native to Central Asia, scattered trees have been planted across New England as ornamentals or for nut production, though they're quite rare in our region.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large round green fruits (husks) about 2 inches across that split open to reveal the familiar brown, wrinkled walnut shell inside. The nuts have that distinctive brain-like surface pattern.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 5-9 smooth-edged leaflets arranged along a central stem. Each leaflet is oval and can be 3-6 inches long, with a slightly leathery texture and aromatic smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, light gray bark on younger trees that develops shallow furrows with age. Much smoother and lighter than the deeply ridged dark bark of black walnut.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male flowers hang in drooping yellow-green catkins 2-4 inches long in spring, while tiny female flowers appear as small clusters at branch tips. Both appear before or with the emerging leaves.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Develops a broad, spreading crown with thick branches. Often planted as a single specimen tree in yards or near buildings rather than growing in forest settings.

habitat: In New England, Persian walnuts are almost exclusively found as planted ornamental or orchard trees in yards, parks, or former homesteads. They prefer well-drained soils and sunny locations, but struggle with our harsh winters and are much less cold-hardy than native walnut species.

seasonality.spring: Yellow-green catkins appear in April-May along with emerging leaves. The compound leaves unfurl relatively late compared to many other trees.
seasonality.summer: Full leafy crown provides dense shade. Green walnut husks develop and mature through the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping. Ripe nuts fall from September through October, often still enclosed in their green husks.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show smooth gray bark and large leaf scars. Persistent nuts or husk fragments may litter the ground beneath.

funFact: Persian walnuts have been cultivated for over 8,000 years, making them one of humanity's oldest tree crops - ancient Persian royalty considered the nuts so valuable that commoners were forbidden from eating them!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with black walnut, but Persian walnut has much smoother, lighter gray bark (versus black walnut's dark, deeply furrowed bark) and leaflets with smooth edges (versus black walnut's saw-toothed leaflets). Memory trick: Persian = smooth and paler.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the 'English walnut' name - these trees aren't from England at all! English merchants just popularized their trade. Also, unlike black walnuts which can inhibit nearby plant growth, Persian walnuts are much more garden-friendly neighbors.
compareHints: Persian walnut differs from our native black walnut and butternut by having smooth-edged leaflets (not serrated), lighter gray bark, and round nuts (butternut has oblong nuts). It's also much less cold-hardy than either native species, explaining why it's so rare in New England compared to warmer growing regions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to butternut, its closest New England relative, black walnut has more leaflets per compound leaf, smooth (not sticky) leaf stems, and rounder nuts versus butternut's elongated nuts.

Among the walnut family members in New England, butternut is easily distinguished from black walnut by its pale gray bark and oblong, sticky-husked nuts versus black walnut's dark bark and round nuts.
Japanese walnut differs from our native black walnut in having a generally more northern cold tolerance and different nut characteristics.
